blocks.orig: With 5,895 metres (19,340 ft), Mount Kilimanjaro is the biggest freestanding mountain in the world and the highest in Africa, shining bright on the map of Tanzania. If you’re planning a trip to this wonderful country, you might be wondering – is Mount Kilimanjaro hard to climb?
blocks.html: Standing 5,895 metres (19,340 ft) tall, Mount Kilimanjaro is Africa’s highest mountain and the largest freestanding mountain on earth, a bright landmark on the map of Tanzania. If a trip to this beautiful country is on your list, you may be asking yourself – how hard is it to climb Mount Kilimanjaro?

blocks.orig: We’re here to give you a solid breakdown of the Kilimanjaro hike difficulty, what you can expect, and how to maximize your chances of reaching the top. We can tell you one thing now – it’s not an easy trek, but it is very much worth it.
blocks.html: Below we explain clearly how difficult the Kilimanjaro hike is, what lies ahead of you and how to give yourself the best possible chance of reaching the summit. One thing we can say straight away – the trek is far from easy, but it is well worth the effort.

blocks.orig: A simple answer: yes. For most people, a Kilimanjaro hike is not a walk in the park. Having said that, the routes themselves are not too challenging. On most treks, there are no steep and difficult climbs to make, but that’s not the real problem here.
blocks.html: The short answer is yes. A Kilimanjaro trek is no walk in the park for most people. That said, the routes are not especially hard in themselves. Most treks involve no steep or technical climbing, yet that is not where the real difficulty lies.

blocks.orig: The actual challenge is dealing with the altitude. The amount of oxygen near the peak is half of what we’re experiencing at sea level, which can take a serious toll on your body if you’re not careful.
blocks.html: What really tests you is the altitude. Close to the summit there is only half as much oxygen as at sea level, and without care this can put your body under heavy strain.

blocks.orig: Another potential hurdle is low temperatures. Despite what most people assume about Africa, they can drop during the hike to rather low values.
blocks.html: Cold can be another obstacle. Contrary to what many people expect from Africa, temperatures on the hike can fall quite low.

blocks.orig: In addition to that, to hike Kilimanjaro, you’ll have to deal with sleeping in tents and having very limited access to amenities for at least five to six days.
blocks.html: On top of this, hiking Kilimanjaro means sleeping in tents and getting by with very few facilities for a minimum of five to six days.

blocks.orig: So even if not very technically demanding, the Kilimanjaro hike is considered hard by most people who’ve tried it.
blocks.html: So although it is not very demanding on a technical level, most people who have done the Kilimanjaro hike describe it as hard.

blocks.orig: The most common issue people encounter when hiking Kilimanjaro is altitude, or more precisely, what low oxygen levels do to a body. At the summit of Kilimanjaro, you will experience approximately 49% of the oxygen that is typically available at sea level. It, very literally, takes your breath away.
blocks.html: The problem hikers on Kilimanjaro run into most often is altitude, or to be exact, the effect of low oxygen levels on the body. On the summit of Kilimanjaro you get roughly 49% of the oxygen normally available at sea level. It quite literally leaves you breathless.

blocks.orig: Such low levels increase the risk of developing altitude sickness that can manifest itself in a variety of unpleasant (and sometimes potentially dangerous) symptoms, such as dizziness, headaches, nausea, and shortness of breath.
blocks.html: Oxygen levels this low raise the chance of altitude sickness, which can show itself through a range of unpleasant (and at times potentially dangerous) symptoms, including dizziness, headaches, nausea and shortness of breath.

blocks.orig: For this reason, one of the most important factors of a successful attempt is acclimatization. Some people take part in special altitude training, which can help them prepare for the hike, but it’s not necessary.
blocks.html: That is why a key factor in a successful climb is acclimatization. Some climbers do dedicated altitude training to get ready for the trek, although this is not essential.

blocks.orig: What you can do is decide on a longer itinerary, with six to nine days for making it to Uhuru Peak. The more time you give yourself, the better. This way, your body can slowly get used to the lower oxygen levels and produce more red blood cells to help with more efficient oxygen distribution in the body.
blocks.html: What you can do is opt for a longer itinerary, taking six to nine days to reach Uhuru Peak. The more time you allow, the better. Your body then has the chance to adapt gradually to the reduced oxygen and to make more red blood cells, so oxygen is spread through your body more efficiently.

blocks.orig: Due to its extreme height, you won’t find any vegetation or fauna on the summit of Kilimanjaro. It also means it’s not safe to spend extended periods of time in this environment, especially without proper acclimatization.
blocks.html: Because it is so extremely high, the summit of Kilimanjaro has no plants or animals. It also means that staying in this environment for long is unsafe, particularly if you have not acclimatised properly.

blocks.orig: So, if you want to try yourself on the mountain, we highly recommend choosing a longer route.
blocks.html: So if you would like to take on the mountain, we strongly advise picking a longer route.

blocks.html: Eight Kilimanjaro routes take you to the summit:

blocks.orig: Depending on which one you choose, you’ll be hiking for five to nine days straight. As we previously pointed out, easier and safer for your body are the longer treks (Machame, Lemosho, Rongai, or Northern Circuit), which take 6+ days to accomplish.
blocks.html: Depending on the route you pick, you will trek for five to nine days straight. As mentioned earlier, the longer treks (Machame, Lemosho, Rongai or Northern Circuit), which need 6+ days to complete, are easier and safer for your body.

blocks.orig: You’ll find companies that advertise and accommodate short routes, which are popular mostly because of their lower price. However, it’s good to be aware of the fact that the success rate on these treks is considerably lower (somewhere close to 60%) compared to the success rate of longer routes, which reaches 85% to 95%.
blocks.html: Some companies promote and run short routes, which are mainly popular because they cost less. It is worth knowing, though, that the success rate on these treks is much lower (around 60%) than on the longer routes, where it reaches 85% to 95%.

blocks.orig: By far the most challenging and dangerous route on Kilimanjaro is the Western Breach route. The reason for that is its steep, rocky slope that has been known to produce bolder avalanches, harming at least six people over the years.
blocks.html: The Western Breach route is by far the hardest and most dangerous on Kilimanjaro. This is because of its steep, rocky slope, which is known to cause boulder avalanches that have injured at least six people over the years.

blocks.orig: The most beginner-friendly trek is the Lemosho route because of its long acclimatisation period and fairly easy hiking experience. It’s also one of the most scenic routes.
blocks.html: For beginners, the best trek is the Lemosho route, thanks to its long acclimatisation period and relatively easy walking. It also ranks among the most scenic routes.

blocks.orig: The Marangu route, which is also called the Coca-Cola route, can be a good choice for first-time Kilimanjaro climbers as well. Not only does it offer huts instead of tents, but also wins trekking novices over with a low level of difficulty. As you might have guessed it, this also makes it one of the busiest treks.
blocks.html: The Marangu route, also known as the Coca-Cola route, is another sound option if you are climbing Kilimanjaro for the first time. It has huts rather than tents and appeals to novice trekkers because it is not very difficult. As you may have guessed, that also makes it one of the most crowded treks.

blocks.orig: None of the Kilimanjaro routes require specialised gear like ropes, harnesses and axes. This doesn’t mean there aren’t any challenging sections on this trek. But, for the majority of the time, the hike is accessible to individuals with varied mountaineering experience.
blocks.html: You do not need specialised equipment such as ropes, harnesses or axes on any of the Kilimanjaro routes. That is not to say the trek has no tough sections. For most of the way, however, the hike is within reach of people with very different levels of mountaineering experience.

blocks.orig: Something to also take into consideration is the sleeping arrangements on the Kilimanjaro hike. All routes, except for Marangu, require hikers to sleep in tents. This, depending on your comfort level and expectations, might be fine or not at all something you wish to endure.
blocks.html: You should also think about where you will sleep on the Kilimanjaro hike. On every route apart from Marangu, hikers sleep in tents. Depending on how comfortable you are with that and what you expect, this may be perfectly fine or something you would rather not put up with.

blocks.orig: Remember – the hike lasts for at least five to six days, and that’s the amount of time you will be forced to sleep on the ground in the sleeping bag and surrounded by other hikers. If that’s not your cup of tea, Marangu is the route for you.
blocks.html: Keep in mind – the trek takes a minimum of five to six days, and for all that time you will sleep on the ground in a sleeping bag with other hikers around you. If that does not appeal to you, choose the Marangu route.

blocks.orig: Access to amenities such as a shower is non-existent. So no, you won’t be able to properly wash yourself for the duration of your hike (but no one minds, really). Toilets, however, are available and regularly cleaned – even if they might be in less than perfect condition on the particularly popular routes.
blocks.html: There are no facilities such as showers at all. So no, you will not be able to wash properly while you are on the hike (although nobody really minds). There are toilets, though, and they are cleaned regularly – even if on the busiest routes they may not be in ideal condition.

blocks.orig: Weather conditions on Kilimanjaro are relatively good, especially during dry seasons. The two windows of time when hiking Kilimanjaro are the safest and most comfortable are from July to October and December through February.
blocks.html: The weather on Kilimanjaro is fairly good, particularly in the dry seasons. The safest and most comfortable periods for hiking Kilimanjaro are July to October and December to February.

blocks.orig: Still, despite the fact that the mountain is located in Africa, due to the altitude, you can expect the temperatures to drop at night to really low values (even -20 degrees Celsius). It’s therefore important to be prepared for it.
blocks.html: Even so, although the mountain lies in Africa, the altitude means night-time temperatures can fall very low (as far as -20 degrees Celsius). Being prepared for this is therefore essential.

blocks.orig: Packing and wearing protective clothing and sleeping in a high-quality, well-insulated sleeping bag can make the experience much more comfortable.
blocks.html: Bringing and wearing protective clothing and sleeping in a good-quality, well-insulated sleeping bag will make the experience far more comfortable.

blocks.orig: High-altitude mountaineering always bears the risk of facing adverse weather conditions, and Kilimanjaro is not an expectation here. But the good news is that during your hike, you’ll be accompanied by experienced guides who’ll be able to ensure your safety and comfort as much as possible.
blocks.html: High-altitude mountaineering always carries the risk of bad weather, and Kilimanjaro is no exception. The good news is that experienced guides will accompany you throughout your hike and do all they can to keep you safe and comfortable.

blocks.orig: How fit do you need to be to climb Kilimanjaro? Well, the simplest way to answer that is to understand what type of endeavour is Kilimanjaro trek.
blocks.html: So how fit must you be to climb Kilimanjaro? The easiest way to answer this is to look at what kind of challenge the Kilimanjaro trek actually is.

blocks.orig: During your hike, you’ll be walking on uneven, sometimes steep terrain for five to nine days consecutively.
blocks.html: On the hike you will walk over uneven and at times steep ground for five to nine days in a row.

blocks.orig: One of the most challenging parts of the whole trek is the summit night, during which you have to face a long and hard uphill slog in the high altitude. After making your way up, you also have to make your way down, all in one day. This equates to up to 15 hours of trekking in relatively challenging terrain and conditions.
blocks.html: Among the toughest parts of the entire trek is the summit night, when you face a long, hard climb at high altitude. Once you have reached the top, you also need to descend again, all within a single day. That adds up to up to 15 hours of trekking over fairly demanding terrain and in tough conditions.

blocks.orig: On top of that, the Kilimanjaro climb can be mentally and emotionally demanding. You’re far away from home, don’t have access to your usual comforts, you sleep in a tent, experience cold, and you’re dependent on your fellow hikers.
blocks.html: The Kilimanjaro climb can also take a mental and emotional toll. You are a long way from home, without your usual comforts, sleeping in a tent, feeling the cold and relying on the people you are hiking with.

blocks.orig: It’s a good idea to prepare your body and mind for this adventure. You may benefit from an intense training regimen (at least four days of training sessions for building endurance and strength).
blocks.html: Preparing both body and mind for this adventure is wise. An intensive training programme (at least four days of sessions to build stamina and strength) may help you.

blocks.orig: Also, make sure your motivation is unshakable. Select a reliable company to organise your hike to ensure your own safety and peace of mind, knowing you’re in good hands.
blocks.html: Make sure, too, that your motivation is rock solid. Choose a trustworthy company to arrange your hike, so you can feel safe and at ease knowing you are in good hands.

blocks.orig: How Difficult Is Kilimanjaro? Success Rates!
blocks.html: How hard is Kilimanjaro? A look at success rates

blocks.orig: As we mentioned earlier, the longer routes offer the highest success rates. A route such as Lemosho has an impressive 90% success rate, whereas a seemingly more popular Marangu route offers only a 65% success rate.
blocks.html: As noted above, the longer routes have the best success rates. The Lemosho route, for example, has an impressive 90% success rate, while the apparently more popular Marangu route reaches only 65%.

blocks.orig: The average success rate for Mount Kilimanjaro is around 65%, which means almost half of all people who try to climb this mountain fail.
blocks.html: On average, around 65% of climbers succeed on Mount Kilimanjaro, so nearly half of everyone who attempts this mountain does not make it.

blocks.orig: Can an Average Person Climb Kilimanjaro?
blocks.html: Is Kilimanjaro within reach of an average person?

blocks.orig: Yes, it’s more than possible for an average, active person to climb Kilimanjaro. A few factors play a role in a successful ascend.
blocks.html: Yes, an average, active person can certainly climb Kilimanjaro. Several factors contribute to a successful ascent.

blocks.orig: Supportive and experienced guide (we’ll take care of that)

blocks.orig: Having solid motivation and a positive attitude

blocks.orig: How many people fail to climb Kilimanjaro?
blocks.html: How many climbers do not reach the top of Kilimanjaro?

blocks.orig: Approximately half to one-third of climbers fail to make it to the summit of Mount Kilimanjaro. There are various reasons for that, the most prominent one being the altitude and the negative effects low oxygen levels have on the body.
blocks.html: Somewhere between a third and a half of climbers do not reach the summit of Mount Kilimanjaro. The reasons vary, but the main one is the altitude and the harmful effect of low oxygen levels on the body.

blocks.orig: No, anyone who is physically active, strong enough, and in good health can climb Kilimanjaro. Age doesn’t play a considerable role here.
blocks.html: No, Kilimanjaro can be climbed by anyone who is physically active, strong enough and healthy. Age is not a major factor.

blocks.orig: Yes, beginners can hike on Kilimanjaro. The important thing is to prepare for this challenge. A person should be in good physical condition, preferably after being in training for at least a couple of months prior to the hike.
blocks.html: Yes, Kilimanjaro is open to beginners. What matters is getting ready for the challenge. You should be in good physical shape, ideally after training for at least a few months before the trek.

blocks.orig: Climbing Kilimanjaro might be one of the hardest things some people will do in their lives, but all the challenges along the way make this experience truly rewarding and one of a kind. As impressive as the mountain is from afar, the views it offers from the summit are just breathtaking.
blocks.html: For some people, climbing Kilimanjaro may rank among the hardest things they ever do, yet the challenges on the way are exactly what make it so rewarding and unique. The mountain looks impressive from a distance, but the views from the summit are simply breathtaking.
